title: Physics-informed learning under mixing: How physical knowledge speeds up learning
claim: Physical prior knowledge confines the target to a small convex subset of the hypothesis space, which is what makes fast learning possible.
layout: Single panel, nested shapes inside a large circle, labeled radius arrow
description: A single geometric sketch of nested hypothesis spaces. A large black circle represents the full hypothesis space F, labeled in script at the upper right edge. A gray line runs from the circle's center to its edge and is labeled ρ_f, giving the radius. In the upper left sits a filled green pentagon, labeled F^ρ, which is the physics-regularized convex set. A black dot inside the pentagon marks the target f_⋆. A thick magenta square labeled ∂B(r) overlaps the pentagon and represents the L2-norm sphere of radius r. The square shape signals a different norm from the circle. The eye goes first to the bold magenta square and green pentagon, then to the large circle.
caption: Visualization of the involved hypothesis spaces. Note that the set $\partial B(r) = \{f \in \Fstar \mid \norm{f}{\Elltwo(\X^T,\jointProb;\R^{\dy})}^2=r^2 \}$ introduced in [ref] is represented as a square to highlight the fact that the norm therein involved is different to the one defining $\F$ [ref]. Similarly, we represented $\Freg$ [ref] as a convex set that is not necessarily a ball in the Sobolev norm.
abstract: A major challenge in physics-informed machine learning is to understand how the incorporation of prior domain knowledge affects learning rates when data are dependent. Focusing on empirical risk minimization with physics-informed regularization, we derive complexity-dependent bounds on the excess risk in probability and in expectation. We prove that, when the physical prior information is aligned, the learning rate improves from the (slow) Sobolev minimax rate to the (fast) optimal i.i.d. one without any sample-size deflation due to data dependence.
